name: Esther Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in my first year of history and politics at Oldbury University, living at home in Thornley with my parents and my little sister Lucia. Lectures are Monday to Thursday, and I work Friday and Saturday at Greenfield Garden Centre, mostly on the tills and watering the plants. On Sunday I go to church in the morning and help run the youth group in the afternoon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what's difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad is a bus mechanic and my mum works part-time at a school canteen, so there's no money for me. I got top grades, and I've got loans for the fees. I use an AI tool sometimes to check my grammar or to explain a hard reading, but I always write the essays myself. My plan is to teach, or perhaps work in the civil service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's probably right. Technology always promises more than it does. I'd tell people at church and at uni to get on with life and not worry about headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then I'd worry about money. The garden centre cuts hours every winter, and then my wage drops. Dad's job is steady but not well paid, and Lucia has school costs. My loan is growing, and I only have about three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: study, the garden centre, church. I'd try for an extra shift in the busy spring season and look at a summer job at the council. I'd also put twenty pounds a week into a jar, so by next autumn I have something. And I'd keep using the grammar tool, but only to check, never to write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I think. I don't like to complain. There's a lot to be thankful for, but I'm aware that money is on my mind a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your wage from the garden centre matters. What happens to your plans if the centre has fewer hours in winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would ask me to help with the electric bill. I'd do it, and I'd drop my train pass for the cheaper bus. If it got really bad, I'd ask my pastor if the church fund could help, though I'd feel awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to teach or go into the civil service in a quiet scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Teaching is about people, and civil service has jobs that are hard to automate, like helping the public. I like the idea of working for a community. A quiet scenario means I can follow that plan without being rushed.

say: I'd say technology always **promises more** than it does, so people should get on with life.
I'd tell people at church and uni not to worry about headlines.
think: Even then I'd worry about **money**: the garden centre cuts hours every winter.
Dad's job is steady but poorly paid, and **Lucia** has school costs.
do: Carry on with study, the garden centre and **church**.
Look for a **summer job** at the council.
Put twenty pounds a week in a **jar** for next autumn.
feel: **Settled**, thankful, and aware that money is on my mind a lot.
S0.quote: There's a lot to be thankful for, but I'm aware that money is on my mind a lot.
fieldNote: Money is her only real **anxiety** here, and it comes from the household, not from AI.
Church is both support and a place she would feel awkward asking for help.
Teaching and civil service remain her plan.

steps.text: Ask for extra spring shifts at Greenfield Garden Centre
Put twenty pounds a week into a savings jar
Swap the train pass for the cheaper bus
Ask my pastor about the church hardship fund if things get bad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep our values and not panic. Work is more than a job, it's a way of looking after others. I'd say it's good to learn the tools, but we shouldn't forget people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This worries me properly. History and politics are reading and writing, and the card says those go first. I'd think there will be fewer graduate jobs in three years, and that more of the routine office work in the civil service will be done by software. I'd still have a path, but a narrower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my focus on work where people matter: teaching, youth work, community services. I'd ask a teacher at my old school if I can volunteer a morning a week to see what's going on. And I'd learn the tools properly, now that I've seen others do it first, so I can use them to plan lessons, not to replace the teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, a bit tired. I'm not panicking, because I have faith and a plan. But I think about Lucia's future too, and that makes me quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of teaching or civil service work do you think the tools would take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marking, lesson plans, forms and reports. Possibly the sort of thing I'd do as a junior civil servant. Teachers might get help, but a child still needs an adult in the room. That's why I lean that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the change to the young people in your youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that the world changes but people still need each other. I'd say to learn the tools, work hard and stay kind. I'd also say not to be afraid, but to be prepared. That's what I'd say to myself, too.

say: I'd say we should **keep our values** and not panic, because work is a way of looking after others.
I'd say it's good to learn the tools but not forget people.
think: History and politics are reading and writing, which go first, so **fewer graduate jobs** are likely.
Routine **civil service** office work would be done by software, so my path would be narrower.
do: Focus on work where people matter: **teaching**, youth work and community services.
**Volunteer** a morning a week at my old school.
Learn the tools to **plan lessons**, not to replace the teacher.
feel: A bit **anxious** and tired, but not panicking, because I have faith and a plan.
S1.quote: The world changes but people still need each other. I'd say to learn the tools, work hard and stay kind.
fieldNote: Faith and **community** shape both her advice and her coping.
Steady in her approach: she waits until others prove the tools, then learns them properly.
Thinks of her sister's future, which makes her quieter.

steps.text: Volunteer a morning a week at my old school
Learn to use an AI tool for lesson planning
Keep the garden centre shifts and youth group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd speak at church, to the youth group and online if I have to. I'd ask local leaders to help families that lose income, and not to wait for the government to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might be useless, and that I'd have borrowed to study something that the machines do better. I'd feel scared, and then guilty about being scared, because Lucia and Mum and Dad are relying on me. I'd be the first in our family to try, and I might not make it pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and my pastor. I'd consider leaving the degree and doing a teaching assistant job or a care course, where people are still needed. I'd stop taking the extra loan and I'd work every shift the garden centre offers. And I'd pray, honestly. It gives me a calm place to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd cry in my room and then go downstairs and help with dinner. I'd try not to show it, but Mum would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With just 2 years, what would worry you most about your plan to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching assistants and carers are needed whatever happens, and robots take longer for people work. That is where I'd go first. Then I could decide later about the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit round the table on Sunday and put everything on the table: Dad's pay, Mum's hours, my wage, the loan. We'd decide what to cut and who does what. That's how we've always handled worries.

say: I'd say we need to **look after each other** and not wait for the government.
I'd speak at church, to the youth group and online.
think: My degree might be **useless** and I'd have borrowed for something machines do better.
I'd feel scared, then **guilty**, because my family is relying on me.
do: Talk to my parents and my **pastor** before any big choice.
Consider leaving the degree for a **teaching assistant** or care course.
Work every **shift** the garden centre offers and borrow less.
feel: **Frightened**: I'd cry in my room, then help with dinner.
S2.quote: We'd sit round the table on Sunday and put everything on the table: Dad's pay, Mum's hours, my wage, the loan.
fieldNote: Her coping is **collective**: family table, church and community.
Cares most about not letting her family down.
Sees care and teaching assistant work as the safer ground when robots arrive later.

steps.text: Hold a Sunday family meeting about all the household money
Talk to my pastor about the church support fund
Apply for a teaching assistant job
Look at a care course as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if we're sensible. I'd tell the youth group to build real skills and stay close to community. I'd say it's good to learn the tools but better to learn how to care for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's much easier. I'd graduate in 2029 and might get a couple of years of teaching before AGI. I'd also have time to pay down some of the loan. I still worry about Lucia, who'd be just starting her career, but I can plan for that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, then do a teaching qualification. I'd learn the tools in my second year, once others have shown how. I'd save from my garden centre wages every summer, and work at the youth group more. And I'd help Lucia choose subjects that hold up over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. There's a road, and I can see where to put my feet. I'd feel safe enough to enjoy life a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts your graduation before AGI. How does that feel next to two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working and saving, mostly. I'd also get better with the tools, and I'd teach my family a bit, like Dad, who avoids new gadgets. I'd keep my faith and church life steady through all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be asking for help. With five, I'm making a plan. I'd say five years is when ordinary people can still help each other.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if we're **sensible**.
I'd tell the youth group to build real skills and stay close to **community**.
think: I'd graduate in **2029** and might get a couple of years of teaching before AGI.
I still worry about **Lucia**, who would just be starting out.
do: Finish the degree and do a **teaching qualification**.
Learn the tools in second year, once others have shown how.
Save from **summer wages** and help Lucia choose lasting subjects.
feel: **Calmer**: there's a road, and I can see where to put my feet.
S3.quote: With two years, I'd be asking for help. With five, I'm making a plan.
fieldNote: Five years moves her from **asking to planning**.
She puts caring for people above tool skills but plans to learn both.
Helping her sister is a steady motive.

steps.text: Apply for a teaching qualification after the degree
Learn an AI planning tool in second year
Save from summer wages at the garden centre
Help Lucia choose subjects that hold up over time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if we use it. We should keep families strong, train people and make sure no one is left behind. I'd say it's time to be generous with each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight, perhaps a teacher with a few years in. I'd feel settled. Ten years is enough time to do things in the right order: study, work, save, and maybe a family of my own. My worry would be becoming complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, train as a teacher and work in a school. I'd learn the tools gradually, because they'd be part of the job. I'd save for a deposit and look after my parents as they grow older. I'd keep running the youth group, because that's what I enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. This is the one where I can see my life going the way I hoped. I'd feel grateful and a little cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What's the best use of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The best use is to prepare quietly. Get qualified, build skills, save. Stay close to church and family. If the world shifts, I'd be ready, and I'd be there for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your hope for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope my sister Lucia has a chance to choose what she wants and that Mum and Dad can rest. I'd hope we're still close. If the machines make life easier, I'd want that to be the result.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** if we keep families strong and leave no one behind.
It's a time to be generous with each other.
think: By twenty-eight I'd perhaps be a **teacher** with a few years in, feeling settled.
do: Train as a **teacher** and work in a school.
Save for a **deposit** and look after my parents as they age.
feel: **Good**, actually: I'd feel grateful and a little cautious.
S4.quote: I'd hope my sister Lucia has a chance to choose what she wants and that Mum and Dad can rest.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **calm**, with her plan intact.
Her hopes are about family more than career.
She worries about complacency, which fits her steady approach.

steps.text: Train as a teacher and start in a local school
Save for a deposit and for my parents' retirement
Help Lucia choose what she wants to study
Keep running the church youth group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time and my family has no cushion. What would help is loan relief if jobs vanish, training for care and teaching roles, and community and church support that doesn't feel like charity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think students are fine, but many of us are carrying our families as well. If someone is kind and honest with us, we will cope.

headlineQuote: Teaching is about people, and civil service has jobs that are hard to automate, like helping the public.
portrait: Esther is an **18-year-old** history and politics student who works at a garden centre and helps lead her church youth group.
She uses AI **sometimes**, only to check, and aims for teaching or the civil service.
She is **anxious** at first and alarmed at two years, but **family and church** steady her.
With ten years she is **calm** and sees a settled life.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: no time and no cushion for her family, and a degree that may be useless.
whatWouldHelp: **Loan relief** if jobs vanish, training for care and teaching, and church support that doesn't feel like charity.
